skill.description: Guides secure authorization for Mailtrap APIs, including token scopes, auth headers, environment variables, and account ID resolution.
skill.summary: Securely configure Mailtrap API tokens, headers, and account IDs for email and account endpoints.

security_audit.summary: The static findings are mostly Markdown formatting, first-party Mailtrap URLs, and documentation examples rather than executable skill code. I found no prompt injection or malicious exfiltration intent, but the curl examples can expose expanded bearer tokens in process arguments or traced CI output. The account ID one-liner also risks selecting the wrong account when a token can access several accounts.

remediation.issue: Curl examples place bearer tokens in command arguments.
remediation.suggestion: Add a warning about process lists and shell tracing, or replace curl snippets with safer SDK or config-file examples.

remediation.issue: The account ID helper selects the first returned account.
remediation.suggestion: Show filtering by account name or access level as the default, not only as a warning.

remediation.issue: Markdown examples trigger many command-execution false positives.
remediation.suggestion: Keep commands clearly marked as examples and state that the skill never runs them automatically.

semantic_findings.title: Token Exposure in Curl Command Examples
semantic_findings.description: Several curl examples expand MAILTRAP_API_TOKEN or MAILTRAP_SANDBOX_API_TOKEN inside Authorization headers. Expanded values can appear in process arguments or traced CI output, which conflicts with the skill warning about command-line token leaks.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The examples pass bearer tokens through shell-expanded curl arguments. The file itself states command-line tokens can leak through ps and CI logs, so this is a concrete documentation risk.

semantic_findings.title: First Account Selection Can Target the Wrong Account
semantic_findings.description: The account ID helper selects the first account returned by the API. A token with access to several accounts could use the wrong account unless the user filters by name or access level.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The one-liner uses the first returned account ID, and the same file warns that multi-account tokens need filtering. The nearby warning reduces severity but does not remove the risky default example.

content.value_statement: Mailtrap API calls fail when tokens, scopes, or account IDs are wrong. This skill explains safe authorization patterns for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code workflows.
actual_capabilities: Explains which Mailtrap token scope to use for sending, sandbox, and account APIs.
Compares Bearer and Api-Token headers for Mailtrap requests.
Defines standard environment variable names for tokens and account IDs.
Shows how to resolve a Mailtrap account ID from the Accounts API.
Lists common authorization mistakes and safer fixes.
limitations: Does not create, rotate, or revoke Mailtrap API tokens.
Does not verify permissions inside a live Mailtrap account.
Requires users to provide their own Mailtrap account and token.
Example requests may need adjustment for each project or CI system.

output_examples.input: I need to call the Contacts API and avoid token mistakes.
output_examples.output: Use an account-level Mailtrap token, a single Bearer header, and the correct account ID for that organization.

output_examples.input: My sandbox test uses my live sending token.
output_examples.output: Use a separate sandbox token. Keep sandbox and live sending tokens isolated to reduce accidental production impact.
Check that the token can access the target account and has admin or owner permissions for write operations.

best_practices: Use the narrowest Mailtrap token scope that supports the task.
Store tokens in environment variables, CI secrets, or a real secret manager.
Resolve account IDs per environment instead of copying them between accounts.
anti_patterns: Do not hardcode Mailtrap tokens in source files, notebooks, or prompts.
Do not mix sandbox tokens with live sending tokens.
Do not assume the first returned account is always the intended account.

faq.question: Which Mailtrap auth header should I use?
faq.answer: Use the Bearer authorization header for new code. Use Api-Token only for older clients that require it.

faq.question: Do all Mailtrap endpoints need an account ID?
faq.answer: Most account-scoped endpoints need one. Some send hosts do not include account_id in the path.

faq.question: Can I use one token for every Mailtrap API?
faq.answer: Use narrower tokens when possible. Separate sandbox, live sending, and account-level access to limit damage from leaks.

faq.question: Where should I store Mailtrap tokens?
faq.answer: Use environment variables, encrypted CI secrets, or a secret manager. Never paste literal tokens into prompts or code.

faq.question: Why did my request return 403?
faq.answer: The token may lack scope, account access, or write permission. Check account ID and access level before retrying.

faq.question: Does this skill send email by itself?
faq.answer: No. It explains authorization patterns and examples. Users still control whether requests are executed.
